To order at a café and ask for the bill.
To use the irregular verbs “a bea” (to drink), “a mânca” (to eat) and “a lua” (to take).
To form the plural of nouns (-i, -e, -uri).
To make double negatives: nu… nimic, nu… nimeni, nu… niciodată.
To use the pronouns “îl, o, îi, le” (him, her, them).
On Friday evening, Radu invites Nora to “Ceasul”, a small café in the old town. The owner, Mr Grigore Bălan, used to be a watchmaker; there are dozens of old clocks on the walls.
Good evening, Radu! Your usual table? And who is the young lady?
Good evening, Mr Grigore! This is Nora, my grandmother’s tenant. She’s an architect from Sweden.
Pleased to meet you! So many clocks! Do they all work?
All of them, miss. I repair them myself, every single one. What can I bring you?
I’ll have a mint tea, please. I never drink coffee in the evening.
A beer for me, please. And shall we eat something sweet? Do you have papanași today?
I do. They’re warm, with sour cream and blueberry jam.
Papanași? What are papanași? I don’t know them.
You don’t know them?! Then we’ll have two portions. Nobody leaves Cluj without papanași!
Mmm… They’re delicious! I’ve never eaten anything like it.
The bill, please! And no, Nora, you’re not paying anything. Today it’s my treat.
All right, but next time I’ll pay. And I’ll show you how to make a real Swedish coffee.
Radu! (the form used to call someone named Radu)
to go, to work: ele merg (they work)
to take: eu iau (I take, I’ll have)
papanași (dessert made with cheese, fried or boiled)
“mânca”, “smântână”: “â” is pronounced like “î”, a deep sound in the middle of the mouth.
“iau” is a single syllable, like “yow” in English. “beau” is also one syllable.
In exclamations, the voice rises on the first word: “Ce de ceasuri!”, “Ce frumos!”.
When you call someone, the name can change: Radu → “Radule!”, domn → “domnule!”, doamnă → “doamnă!”. The stress stays on the same syllable.
1. Three irregular verbs: a bea, a mânca, a lua
Notice the vowel change in “a mânca”: “â” becomes “ă” for eu, tu, el, ei (mănânc), but stays “â” for noi and voi (mâncăm). Romanian often has vowel alternations like this.
I’ll have a tea. (at a café: “iau” = I order)
The Romanian plural has several endings. The most common are -i, -e and -uri. The safest thing is to learn each word with its plural.
The -i plural often changes the consonant before it: student → studenți, frate → frați, brad → brazi, cald → calzi. Listen carefully.

In Romanian, negative words (nimic – nothing, nimeni – nobody, niciodată – never, nicăieri – nowhere) ALWAYS also need “nu” before the verb. Two negatives don’t make a positive as in English: they reinforce the negation.
Even when the negative word comes first, “nu” stays: “Nimeni nu pleacă din Cluj fără papanași!” (Nobody leaves Cluj without papanași!)
4. Him, her: the pronouns îl, o, îi, le
When you replace a direct object (whom? what?), you use short pronouns placed BEFORE the verb.
For people, Romanian uses “pe” before the object: “O invit pe Nora” (I invite Nora), “Îl cunosc pe Radu” (I know Radu). The short pronoun is repeated even when the name is there.
With “nu”, the pronoun is often joined to it: “nu îi cunosc” → “nu-i cunosc”, “nu îl văd” → “nu-l văd”.
In Romania tipping is normal: usually 10% of the bill. You can say “Păstrați restul” (keep the change) if you want to leave the change for the waiter.
At the table: “Poftă bună!” at the start and “Noroc!” when you clink glasses. At the end you tell the host: “Mulțumesc, a fost delicios!” (Thank you, it was delicious!).
What are you drinking? Coffee or tea?
“Do you repair the clocks?” – “Yes, I repair ___.”
All the clocks work. Mr Grigore repairs every single one.
I never go to cafés. Tomcats don’t drink coffee and nobody gives them papanași. But today I hear an interesting story.
It’s Saturday morning. Nora tells everyone at breakfast: “Grigore’s café has fifty-three clocks. They all work. All except one.”
Mrs Pop puts her cup down on the table. “The big clock by the door?” she asks.
Mrs Pop doesn’t answer straight away. She looks out of the window. Then she says quietly: “I know it. That clock is from my husband, from Vasile.”
Nora says nothing. I say nothing. Even the fridge says nothing.

“Vasile and Grigore were very good friends,” Mrs Pop goes on. “Vasile gives him the clock a month before… before he leaves us. Grigore has been repairing it for ten years. But the clock doesn’t want to work.”
“Maybe it doesn’t want to work without Vasile,” says Nora.
Mrs Pop smiles, but her eyes are wet. “Maybe.”
Then she gets up and makes another coffee. For her, not for me. I only get a stroke on the head.
But it’s a long stroke. And sometimes that’s better than papanași.
In the evening, when Nora comes home, I sit by the door and wait for her. That’s what real friends do.
to know: dumneavoastră știți (you know, formal)
“să plece” = to leave, here: to die (said gently)

Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. Tap any word to see what it means. Four questions follow at the end.
My name is Grigore Bălan. I am seventy-one years old.
For forty years I was a watchmaker. I used to repair clocks in a small workshop on Matei Corvin Street.
Now I have a café. It’s called “Ceasul” (The Clock), of course.
My customers drink coffee, tea and wine. They eat papanași and homemade cakes.
I never drink coffee after four o’clock. I only drink lime-blossom tea.
On the walls I have fifty-three clocks. I repair them all, every morning.
They all work, except one. That one I can’t repair. Not yet.
watchmaker (a craftsman who repairs clocks and watches)
“reparam” = past tense of “a repara” (I used to repair)
Matthias Corvinus (king of Hungary, born in Cluj)
lime tree, linden (a tree with fragrant flowers; lime-blossom tea)
to be able to: eu pot (I can)
